qs.q: A patient develops an excessive scar following a burn injury, but histopathological examination confirms that the excess collagen deposition remains strictly confined within the original boundaries of the wound. What is this condition called?
qs.e: A hypertrophic scar is characterized by excessive collagen confined within the original wound margin, differentiating it from a keloid which extends beyond the original margins. Both represent complications of aberrant wound healing.
qs.s: General Pathology Revision: Cell Injury, Inflammation & Adaptation: MCQs

qs.q: Laparoscopy in a patient with chronic pelvic pain reveals blue-black 'powder-burn' lesions on the pelvic peritoneum and chocolate cysts on the ovaries. What is the definitive diagnostic histological finding?
qs.e: Uterine endometriosis is diagnosed by identifying ectopic endometrial glands and stroma, often accompanied by haemosiderin-laden macrophages. Signet-ring cells are characteristic of Krukenberg tumours, not endometriosis.
qs.s: Female & Male Genital Pathology: Ulcers, HPV, Endometriosis,: MCQs

qs.q: An immunocompromised patient develops a severe burn wound infection characterized by a blue-green pigment production. Which organism is the most likely cause?
qs.e: Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces a characteristic blue-green pigment (pyocyanin) and commonly causes burn wound infections. Klebsiella pneumoniae typically causes pneumonia with thick mucoid colonies.

qs.q: Which specific type of secondary peptic ulcer is classically associated with severe burn injuries?
o: Cushing ulcer secondary to brain injury
Curling ulcer secondary to burn injury
qs.e: Curling ulcers are secondary peptic ulcers that develop in response to severe burn injuries. Cushing ulcers, by contrast, result from intracranial lesions.
qs.s: Gastritis and Peptic Ulcer Disease: MCQs

qs.q: What mechanism explains the formation of stress ulcers caused by severe burns or head injuries?
o: Direct bacterial colonization and destruction of the duodenal mucosa
Intense vasoconstriction of gastric mucosa vasculature leading to sloughing
Hypersecretion of gastrin secondary to an endocrine pancreatic tumor
Permanent inhibition of mucosal prostaglandin synthesis by endogenous toxins
qs.e: Stress ulcers are caused by severe burns or head injury via intense vasoconstriction of the vasculature supplying the gastric mucosa, leading to cell sloughing and ulceration. NSAIDs act instead by inhibiting prostaglandin production.

qs.q: A critically ill patient in the intensive care unit following severe burns develops an inflamed gallbladder without any evidence of cystic or common bile duct obstruction. What is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acute acalculous cholecystitis in an ischemic basis
Choledochal cyst infection within dilated ducts
Primary sclerosing cholangitis of the biliary tree
qs.e: Acute acalculous cholecystitis is an inflamed gallbladder in the absence of an obstructed duct, typically occurring in critically ill patients due to an ischemic basis. Ascending cholangitis requires an obstruction of the biliary tree with infection.

qs.q: A patient with severe burns shows elevated serum levels of cardiac troponin despite no chest pain. This finding indicates:
o: Loss of plasma membrane integrity in cardiac myocytes
Increased synthesis of troponin due to stress
qs.e: Troponins are intracellular proteins released into circulation when plasma membrane integrity is lost during necrosis. Their detection indicates membrane damage and cell death, not increased synthesis. While burns can cause cardiac stress, elevated troponin specifically reflects membrane rupture and protein leakage—a hallmark of necrosis.
qs.s: Pathology MCQs: Cell Injury, Cell Death, and Adaptations

qs.q: A 39-year-old man incurs a burn injury to his hands and arms while working on a propane furnace. Over the next 3 weeks, the burned skin heals without the need for skin grafting. Which of the following is the most critical factor in determining whether the skin in the region of the burn will regenerate?
o: Good cardiac output with tissue perfusion
qs.e: The skin appendages have epithelium from which the surface epidermis can regenerate. A partial thickness burn retains epithelial elements in the skin. This is why a full thickness burn is much worse and requires grafting.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Burns are tissue injuries from heat, chemicals, electricity or radiation that disrupt skin integrity, fluid balance and immune function. Clinical reasoning focuses on assessing depth, extent, and systemic impact to guide resuscitation, infection control and rehabilitation.

sections.p: A burn is a loss of skin integrity due to an external agent. Diagnosis is clinical, based on appearance, depth, and total body surface area (TBSA).
Severity is staged by depth and TBSA. The Lund‑Browder chart estimates TBSA; the ABCDE system guides resuscitation.
b: First‑degree: superficial epidermis, <10% TBSA; second‑degree: epidermis + dermis, <20% TBSA; third‑degree: full thickness, >20% TBSA

sections.p: Common causes vary by setting. In low‑resource areas, open fire, cooking stoves, kerosene, and electrical accidents are frequent.
b: Thermal: open flame, hot liquids, cooking fires

sections.p: Patients present with pain, erythema, blistering, or dry scarring. Systemic signs include tachycardia, hypotension, and altered mental status.
Investigations confirm extent, rule out complications and guide fluid resuscitation.

t.b: Abnormal values indicate fluid shifts or organ injury

sections.p: Early recognition of shock, inhalation injury, and infection prevents mortality.
Treat the cause, stabilize the patient, prevent infection, and support healing.
b: Secure airway if inhalation injury suspected
Apply sterile dressings, avoid tight bandages
Use broad‑spectrum antibiotics if infection risk high

t.b: Avoid nephrotoxic agents in renal impairment

sections.p: Long‑term care includes wound care, physiotherapy, and psychosocial support. Prevention focuses on safe cooking practices and fire safety.
b: Education on fire safety and safe use of kerosene

sections.p: Differential includes superficial skin infections, allergic dermatitis, and scalds from non‑thermal sources.
Lab values may be falsely normal early in shock; skin blanching may mask underlying depth.
b: Early serum lactate may be low despite hypoperfusion
Dry eschar can hide underlying dermal injury

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypotension or tachycardia, signs of inhalation injury, extensive TBSA (>20%), altered mental status, signs of infection such as fever or purulent drainage

faq.q: What is the first step in managing a burn patient?
faq.a: Assess airway, breathing, circulation and estimate TBSA for fluid resuscitation.

faq.q: How do you estimate burn size in children?
faq.a: Use the rule of nines or Lund‑Browder chart, adjusting for age and body proportions.

faq.q: When is surgery needed for burns?
faq.a: For full‑thickness burns, graftable areas, or when infection or contracture threatens function.
